Let me describe the approval rate, because it is the line everybody is asking about. In January, February and March it was flat, at around sixty percent. Nothing moved. In April there was a small dip, to fifty-eight, and that was the first signal. Then the new rule came in at the end of April, and in May approvals fell sharply, by eight points, to fifty-two percent. That was expected. In June the rate rose slightly, to fifty-four. So it has started to recover, but slowly. For the next quarter, we expect approvals to recover gradually and to level off at about fifty-six percent. We do not expect them to go back to sixty, and that is a decision, not a problem.

I ask three questions of every chart I see, and most charts fail at least one of them. The first question is about the axis. Where does it start? If the axis starts at ninety-five instead of zero, a rise of two points looks like a mountain. It is the oldest trick there is, and it still works. The second question is about the start date. Why does the line begin here? If you start a chart at the lowest point of the year, every line looks like a recovery. Somebody chose that date, and you should ask why. The third question is the most important one: compared with what? A rate that rose by two points means nothing on its own. Compared with last year, with the market, or with the plan? Without a comparison, a number is just a number, and a chart is just a picture.
